title: EUR 90,000 MT103 arrived in minutes, the funds took three days
explain:
A EUR 90,000 payment instruction reaches the beneficiary bank in minutes.
The beneficiary calls to ask where the money is.
The funds are still working through the correspondent chain, three days later.

Here's how that happens:

→ MT103 travels fast to the beneficiary bank
→ The funds settle separately through an MT202 COV
→ The MT202 COV waits on correspondent accounts at its own pace
→ The beneficiary bank knows about the payment but holds no funds

The assumption was:
"The instruction arriving means the money arrived."

Why?

The cover method separates the payment instruction from the funds so the MT103 can reach the beneficiary bank fast while settlement works through correspondent accounts at its own pace. Keeping customer details out of the funds leg also protects privacy and keeps the correspondent chain clean. The price is reconciliation: the two legs must match on amount and reference, and any mismatch becomes an exception.

Fast instruction ≠ Fast funds.

BA Takeaway

Reconcile the two legs on amount and reference before anyone is told the money is there.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Instruction received (MT103)
→ Funds settled (MT202 COV)
→ Amount matched across both legs
→ Reference matched across both legs

The real requirement isn't "Did the MT103 arrive?"

It's "What evidence proves the funds leg settled and matched the instruction before the beneficiary is told?"

Have you seen a beneficiary promised money that was still three days away?
takeaway: The price is reconciliation: the two legs must match on amount and reference, and any mismatch becomes an exception.

title: EUR 75,000 payment, no route found, reject or repair?
explain:
A EUR 75,000 payment arrives with no route the system can determine.
The system offers the easy answer: reject it.
A competitor would repair it, find another route, and send it through.
The customer would never know the difference, except in the result.

Here is how that happens:

→ Payment arrives for EUR 75,000
→ Routing cannot be determined automatically
→ Option one: reject, easy, fast, customer loses
→ Option two: repair and reroute, more work, payment succeeds
→ Option three: manual intervention, a person decides

The assumption was:
"When the system cannot route, rejection is the only honest answer."

Rejecting is the easiest answer but not necessarily the best one.

Why?

Each option carries different consequences for customer experience, revenue, operational effort, SLA, risk, and payment success rate. The real choice sits between rejection, repair with alternative routing, and manual intervention, and it is a business choice, not a system default.

Reject is a decision, not a default.

Why does the easy answer cost a customer the bank could have kept?

BA Takeaway

Identify the decision point, frame the options with their impact, and take the decision to the business owner.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Reject, what the customer loses
→ Repair and reroute, what it costs to save the payment
→ Manual intervention, when a person must decide

Show all three options with their impact on experience, revenue, SLA, risk and success rate before anyone picks one.

The real requirement is not "What does the system do when routing is unknown?"

It is "What evidence proves the business chose this outcome, knowing what each option costs?"

Have you seen a payment rejected that a repair could have saved?
takeaway: The most valuable question is what the business wants the system to do when this situation occurs.

title: EUR 45,000 payment, every mandatory field filled, still fails
explain:
A Eurozone customer payment for EUR 45,000 arrives.
Reference, account number and customer name are all filled.
The debtor postal address has no street name.
The payment fails downstream. The form said it was complete.

Here is how that happens:

→ Payment arrives, mandatory fields all present
→ Debtor postal address missing its street name
→ Checks pass, because the street is not mandatory
→ Screening and the debit instruction fail downstream on the missing data

The assumption was:
"If every mandatory field is filled, the payment is meaningful."

Checking only mandatory fields misses the point.

Why?

The debit instruction and the screening of the payment can depend on data that is not mandatory but is relevant in cross-border payments, and a missing street name can look harmless while the payment itself is not meaningful. Some missing fields are business rules that will fail the payment in processing.

Mandatory is not the same as meaningful.

Why does a payment with every mandatory field filled still fail?

BA Takeaway

Ask what happens if the data is missing, and treat a business-critical gap as a failure before it reaches processing.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Mandatory fields, what the form requires
→ Business-critical data, what screening and processing need
→ Downstream impact, rejection, block, or breach of a rule

List the data each downstream step needs, and validate against that list, not only against the mandatory list.

The real requirement is not "Are the mandatory fields filled?"

It is "What evidence proves the payment carries everything processing and screening need?"

Have you seen a payment fail on a field nobody marked mandatory?
takeaway: Some missing fields are business rules that will fail the payment in processing.

explain:
A maker raised a corporate payment of EUR 75,000 in one click.
Workflow approved it.
The supplier never received it.

Here is what happened:

→ Maker initiates the payment
→ Preprocessor checks entitlement, account, limits, fees and payee
→ Workflow approves the payment
→ Bank screening holds it
→ Account never debited, network never clears it, ledger never closes it

The requirement said:
"Once workflow approves, the payment is sent."

So the screen showed approved, and everyone assumed the money was on its way.

Why?

Fifteen steps and nine decisions stand between maker and ledger. Every Yes moves the payment forward, and every No stops or re-routes it. A No at bank screening stops the payment after approval, and an approved payment that never clears is still an unpaid payment.

Approval is not settlement.

BA Takeaway

Approval, screening, debit, clearing and ledger posting are separate stages, so keep them separate:

→ Workflow approval status
→ Bank screening outcome
→ Account debit confirmed
→ Network clearing and ledger posting

The real requirement is not "When was it approved?"

It is "What evidence proves each step completed, including the final ledger posting?"

Have you ever seen an approved payment stall silently at a later step?
takeaway: Approval is not settlement.

title: VND 500,000,000 domestic payment, nothing reaches the rail until the preprocessor clears it
explain:
A corporate in Vietnam sends VND 500,000,000 to a supplier.
The payment sits, unmoving, for hours.
The rail is fine. The beneficiary bank is fine.
The payment never cleared the preprocessor.

Here is how that happens:

→ Corporate initiates the payment
→ Preprocessor, the central control point
→ Payment hub, central processing after the preprocessor
→ NAPAS, the domestic rail in Vietnam
→ Beneficiary bank credits the beneficiary

The assumption was:
"The rail carries the payment, so check the rail first."

In a domestic payment in Vietnam, the payment preprocessor is the central control point.

Why?

The flow runs from the corporate, through the preprocessor, to the payment hub, then NAPAS, then the beneficiary bank. Nothing reaches the rail until the preprocessor has cleared it, so a payment stuck before the rail looks like a rail failure from the outside.

The gate is before the rail.

Why does a payment sit for hours on a rail that is working fine?

BA Takeaway

Check the control point first, and show its decision before the rail status.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Preprocessor decision, cleared or held
→ Payment hub, processing after the preprocessor
→ NAPAS rail, carrying what the preprocessor cleared
→ Beneficiary bank, crediting the beneficiary

Show the preprocessor result on the payment status, with the reason for any hold.

The real requirement is not "Is the rail working?"

It is "What evidence proves the preprocessor cleared this payment?"

Have you blamed a rail for a payment held at the gate before it?
takeaway: Nothing reaches the rail until the preprocessor has cleared it.

title: VND 800,000,000 payment, a duplicate slips past six checks
explain:
A corporate sends VND 800,000,000 in Vietnam.
The same payment is sent twice by mistake.
Six checks pass. The duplicate check is the one that matters.
It catches it, minutes before the money moves twice.

Here is how that happens:

→ Account validation, account exists and is valid
→ Format check, message format is correct
→ Authorisation check, payment is properly authorised
→ Limits, AML and sanctions, all checked
→ Duplicate check, payment is not a repeat
→ Routing and enrichment, then it moves on

The assumption was:
"Any one check is enough. They all check the same thing."

Before a domestic payment moves on, the preprocessor runs the full gate: account, format, authorisation, limits, AML and sanctions, duplicates, routing and enrichment.

Why?

Those checks are the reason a payment can be trusted to reach the right account. Each check catches a different failure, and the duplicate check is the only one that sees a payment sent twice, however valid it looks on every other test.

Seven checks, seven different failures caught.

Why does a perfectly valid payment still need a duplicate check?

BA Takeaway

Run the full gate, in order, and never let a payment skip a check because the others passed.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Account, format and authorisation, is it real and allowed
→ Limits, AML and sanctions, is it permitted
→ Duplicates, has it been sent before
→ Routing and enrichment, where it goes and what it carries

Show all seven check results on the payment, and block on any single failure.

The real requirement is not "Did the payment pass validation?"

It is "What evidence proves every check in the gate ran and passed?"

Have you seen a duplicate caught only by the last check?
takeaway: Those checks are the reason a payment can be trusted to reach the right account.

title: EUR 400,000 cross-border payment, rejected three times, preprocessor was missing
explain:
A bank sends EUR 400,000 across borders.
It is rejected three times.
Each rejection names a different fault.
There was no control tower watching the payment before it left.

Here is how that happens:

→ Payment prepared, no preprocessor in the flow
→ Sent with thin data, no enrichment
→ Compliance check fails downstream
→ Wrong route, rejected again, then rejected a third time

The assumption was:
"Each system checks its own part, so no one needs to watch the whole payment."

In cross-border payments the preprocessor is the control tower: it validates, enriches, checks compliance, routes and processes the payment, so fewer payments are rejected and more go straight through.

Why?

A strong preprocessor is what makes straight-through processing possible. Without it, each fault is found by a different system downstream, and the payment is rejected again and again for faults one gate would have caught together.

One gate, fewer rejections.

Why does the same payment get rejected three times for three different faults?

BA Takeaway

Put the control tower before the rail, and let it catch every fault in one place.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Validate, checks before the payment moves on
→ Enrich, data added for straight-through processing
→ Compliance, checked before routing
→ Route and process, sent down the right rail

Show the preprocessor result, with every check, before the payment leaves the bank.

The real requirement is not "Was the payment sent?"

It is "What evidence proves the payment was validated, enriched and compliance-checked before it left?"

Have you seen a payment rejected again and again for faults one gate would have caught?
takeaway: A strong preprocessor is what makes straight-through processing possible.

title: EUR 250,000 payment fails, every layer says the fault is in another layer
explain:
A EUR 250,000 payment fails.
The technical team blames the data.
The data team blames the business rules.
The business team blames compliance.
Every layer is pointing at another layer.

Here is how that happens:

→ Technical layer, format and transport
→ Payment data layer, fields and values
→ Business layer, rules and limits
→ Compliance layer, screening and sanctions
→ Routing layer, path and destination

The assumption was:
"Validation is one check. Find it and fix it."

Preprocessor validation works in layers: technical, payment data, business, compliance and routing.

Why?

Each layer catches a different kind of error, and the full lifecycle runs from initiation through to settlement and reconciliation. A failure with no layer named is a failure nobody owns, so each team blames the next layer down.

Name the layer, own the fault.

Why does every team blame another layer for the same failed payment?

BA Takeaway

Validate layer by layer, and record which layer caught each fault.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Technical, catches technical errors
→ Payment data, catches payment data errors
→ Business, catches business errors
→ Compliance, catches compliance errors
→ Routing, catches routing errors

Show the layer on every validation failure, with the lifecycle stage beside it.

The real requirement is not "Why did the payment fail?"

It is "What evidence proves which layer caught the fault, and at which lifecycle stage?"

Have you seen five teams blame each other for one failed payment?
takeaway: Each layer catches a different kind of error, and the full lifecycle runs from initiation through to settlement and reconciliation.

title: EUR 600,000 payment enters GPP, vanishes before the rail
explain:
A EUR 600,000 payment enters the payment hub.
It is parsed, validated, mapped and screened.
Then it vanishes.
The rail never sees it, and core banking never posts it.

Here is how that happens:

→ Channel, where the payment starts
→ API gateway and message queue, entry and queuing
→ GPP parse and validate, parsed, validated and duplicate-checked
→ Map to ISO 20022, payment mapped to the rich data standard
→ Compliance screening, screened before routing
→ Route to SWIFT or domestic rail, then acknowledge, post and reconcile

The assumption was:
"Once it is inside GPP, the payment is safe."

From a Tech BA view, a payment flows from the channel through the API gateway and message queue into GPP, where it is parsed, validated, checked for duplicates, mapped to ISO 20022, screened for compliance, routed to a SWIFT or domestic rail, acknowledged, and finally posted to core banking with reconciliation.

Why?

Exceptions are handled at each stage, and a payment can fail at any of them. A flow that is only watched at the channel and at the ledger has a blind middle, and a payment that fails inside GPP looks like it vanished.

Inside the hub is where payments are lost.

Why does a payment disappear between parsing and posting?

BA Takeaway

Handle exceptions at each stage, and show the payment at every stage inside the hub.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Entry, gateway and queue
→ GPP processing, parse, validate, duplicate check, map
→ Compliance screening, before routing
→ Rail, posting and reconciliation, the close of the flow

Show the stage and the exception handler at every step, so no stage is blind.

The real requirement is not "Did the payment enter GPP?"

It is "What evidence proves the payment passed each stage inside GPP?"

Have you lost a payment inside a hub nobody was watching?
takeaway: Exceptions are handled at each stage.

title: EUR 50,000 paid twice, the retry had no idempotency key
explain:
A customer retries a EUR 50,000 payment after a timeout.
The retry succeeds.
So does the first attempt, a second later.
EUR 100,000 leaves the account for a EUR 50,000 payment.

Here is how that happens:

→ First call times out, outcome unknown
→ Customer retries the same payment
→ API has no idempotency protection
→ Both calls post, EUR 50,000 paid twice

The assumption was:
"A retry is safe. The system will know it is the same payment."

A reliable payment API rests on stateless validation, synchronous fraud and risk checks, idempotency, metadata-driven configuration, orchestration, compliance and reconciliation.

Why?

Idempotency matters because a retried call must never create a duplicate payment. Without it, a timeout plus a retry is a duplicate by design, and the second posting is not a system error, it is the missing control.

A retry without idempotency is a second payment.

Why does a careful retry double the payment?

BA Takeaway

Make every payment call idempotent, and prove a retry returns the first result instead of a second payment.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Stateless validation, checked without stored session state
→ Synchronous fraud and risk checks, in line before posting
→ Idempotency, a retried call never creates a duplicate
→ Orchestration, compliance and reconciliation, closing the flow

Show the idempotency key on every payment call, and test the timeout-then-retry path.

The real requirement is not "Did the retry succeed?"

It is "What evidence proves the retry returned the first payment instead of creating a second?"

Have you seen a retry double a payment?
takeaway: Idempotency matters because a retried call must never create a duplicate payment.

title: EUR 5,000 sent abroad, beneficiary receives EUR 4,850, rate never shown
explain:
A customer sends EUR 5,000 abroad.
The beneficiary receives EUR 4,850.
The customer was never shown the rate, the fees, or how long the rate held.
The price was agreed after the fact, which is no agreement at all.

Here is how that happens:

→ Customer pays in a different currency, EUR 5,000
→ Rate and fees not shown clearly before confirmation
→ Rate changes before the payment completes
→ Beneficiary credited a different amount, customer cannot reconcile it

The assumption was:
"The rate at the time is the rate the customer agreed to."

When a customer pays in a different currency, they need to see the exchange rate, the fees, how long the rate is valid, and the exact amount the beneficiary will receive.

Why?

If the rate changes or the fees are not shown clearly, the beneficiary is credited a different amount and the customer cannot reconcile the payment. Transparency means showing the total cost and the applied rate before the customer confirms, because a price agreed after the fact is no agreement at all.

A price shown after is not a price agreed.

Why does the beneficiary receive EUR 4,850 for a EUR 5,000 payment?

BA Takeaway

Show the full deal upfront, rate, fees, validity and beneficiary amount, before confirmation.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Exchange rate, shown before confirmation
→ Fees, shown in full
→ Rate validity, how long the rate holds
→ Beneficiary amount, the exact amount to be received

Lock the rate for its stated validity, and show all four figures on the confirmation screen.

The real requirement is not "What rate applied?"

It is "What evidence proves the customer saw the full deal before confirming?"

Have you sent money abroad and found the beneficiary short?
takeaway: Transparency means showing the total cost and the applied rate before the customer confirms.

title: EUR 30,000 to a supplier, paid in full, cannot be matched to any invoice
explain:
A company pays a supplier EUR 30,000.
The money arrives in full.
The supplier cannot match it to any invoice.
The payment carries no structured remittance data, so the cash sits unallocated.

Here is how that happens:

→ Payment sent for EUR 30,000, payer, beneficiary and purpose attached
→ Remittance data unstructured or incomplete
→ Supplier cannot match the payment to the invoice
→ Screening cannot run properly on the thin data

The assumption was:
"Data quality is a formatting preference."

Every cross-border payment carries payer, beneficiary, purpose and remittance data that the supplier needs to allocate the cash and that compliance screening depends on.

Why?

If the data is unstructured or incomplete, the supplier cannot match the payment to the invoice and the screening cannot run properly. Structured data is what makes a payment reconcilable and compliant at the same time, so data quality is a payment control, not a formatting preference.

Unstructured data is unallocated cash.

Why does a payment that arrived in full sit unallocated?

BA Takeaway

Treat structured data as a payment control, and validate it before the payment leaves.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Payer and beneficiary data, who sent and who receives
→ Purpose data, why the payment was made
→ Remittance data, what the supplier needs to allocate cash
→ Compliance screening, what runs on the structured data

Require structured remittance data on every cross-border payment, and reject what cannot be matched.

The real requirement is not "Did the money arrive?"

It is "What evidence proves the supplier can allocate it and screening can run on it?"

Have you paid a supplier in full and still been chased for the invoice?
takeaway: Structured data is what makes a payment reconcilable and compliant at the same time.

title: The reject reason the customer must never see
explain:
A EUR 50,000 payment is rejected.

Inside the bank, the reason is precise: the account is closed.

The customer is told the same words. In that country, sharing it breaks the privacy rules.

Here is how it happens:

→ Payment is rejected
→ Internal reason recorded: account closed
→ Privacy rules differ by country
→ The reason is shown to the customer without a country check
→ Sensitive information is exposed

The requirement said:
"Show the customer the reject reason."

Why?

The internal diagnostic reason can be precise and sensitive, and privacy rules differ by country. A reason that is safe to show in one country can be a breach in another.

Precise inside, careful outside.

BA Takeaway

The bank must configure what reason is shown, at what scope and through which channel, so the customer gets a useful explanation without exposing sensitive information.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Internal diagnostic reason
→ Country privacy rule
→ Channel and scope of what is shown

The real requirement is not "What reason do we show?"

It is "What evidence proves the customer was told enough, without exposing what must stay private?"

Have you seen a reject reason shared with a customer that should never have left the bank?
takeaway: Precise inside, careful outside. The reason shown must pass the privacy rule first.

title: The EUR 150,000 payment that could not go instant
explain:
A customer sends a EUR 150,000 instant payment.

The customer limit allows it. The scheme maximum does not.

The payment cannot go as an instant payment at all.

Here is how it happens:

→ Customer submits a EUR 150,000 instant payment
→ Customer limit check passes
→ Scheme maximum check fails
→ The payment cannot go instant, whatever the customer limit says
→ It must be rerouted to a standard transfer

The requirement said:
"Apply the customer limit."

Why?

The scheme maximum and the customer limit are two different numbers, and an older internal guide still carries the old scheme figure after the regulation changed it. The product configuration and the routing rules were never updated together.

The scheme maximum is the hard gate, not the customer limit.

BA Takeaway

A payment above the scheme maximum cannot go as an instant payment at all. Update the configuration and the routing rules together, and check the guide against the current regulation.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Scheme maximum
→ Customer limit
→ Routing rule

The real requirement is not "What is the customer limit?"

It is "What evidence proves the scheme figure in the system matches the current regulation?"

Have you seen a payment fail because an old guide still carried the old scheme maximum?
takeaway: The scheme maximum is the hard gate, not the customer limit.

title: The customer asked for Citi, the payment went through Chase
explain:
A customer sends a USD 250,000 payment and names Citi New York as intermediary.

The payment routes through Chase New York.

Nobody changed the instruction. A standing rule overruled it.

Here is how it happens:

→ Customer instruction names Citi New York
→ Standing Settlement Instruction names Chase New York
→ Engine applies the SSI
→ Payment routes through Chase New York
→ A reference data update does not displace the rule

The assumption was:
"The instruction decides the route."

Why?

Routing precedence puts the Standing Settlement Instruction ahead of a conflicting customer instruction, because an SSI is a settlement instruction agreed in advance between banks, naming the preferred correspondent for a currency and counterparty.

Routing follows the governing rule, not the message alone.

BA Takeaway

A different intermediary requires the SSI to be updated first, or an explicit override in the payment message. Routing follows the governing rules as much as the message itself.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Customer instruction
→ Standing Settlement Instruction
→ Explicit override in the message

The real requirement is not "What did the customer ask for?"

It is "What evidence proves which rule governed the route?"

Have you seen a payment take a route nobody in the instruction asked for?
takeaway: Routing follows the governing rule, not the message alone. Update the SSI first, or override explicitly.

title: EUR 5 million valid on Monday, failed on Friday
explain:
A EUR 5 million payment is accepted on Monday for Friday execution, against a EUR 6 million balance.

By Friday it fails.

Nothing was wrong on Monday. Everything moved in between.

Here is how it happens:

→ EUR 5 million accepted Monday for Friday execution
→ Payment is warehoused
→ Balance, account details, sanctions status and cut-off times move before Friday
→ Friday arrives, and the payment is not re-validated
→ Execution fails

The assumption was:
"Accepted means it will execute."

Why?

Warehousing turns a future-dated payment into a commitment to execute, not merely a stored instruction. Validity on Monday proves nothing about Friday.

Warehousing is a commitment to re-check, not a guarantee.

BA Takeaway

Re-validate on balance, account status, sanctions and cut-offs at execution, then execute or reject. Warehousing is risk management across the interval.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Acceptance checks on Monday
→ Execution checks on Friday
→ Balance, sanctions and cut-off position

The real requirement is not "Was the payment accepted?"

It is "What evidence proves the payment is still valid at execution?"

Have you seen a warehoused payment fail on the day it was meant to go out?
takeaway: Warehousing is a commitment to re-check, not a guarantee. Re-validate at execution.

title: 3,000 payments arrived at once, and the SLA broke on sequencing
explain:
Thousands of payments arrive together.

Every control runs in sequence. The SLA breaks.

The checks were all correct. The order was wrong.

Here is how it happens:

→ Thousands of payments arrive together
→ Every control runs one after another
→ Compliance takes 3 seconds, fraud takes 4 seconds, run in sequence they take 7
→ The SLA is missed
→ Payments queue behind checks that could have run together

The assumption was:
"Run every control in order."

Why?

Control design is a business decision about ordering, not a technical default. If the account is closed and rejection is the defined outcome, the payment can go to rejection once the account check is done. Compliance and fraud can run in parallel, so checks of 3 and 4 seconds finish in 4 seconds together instead of 7 in sequence.

Control order is a business decision, not a technical default.

BA Takeaway

Spell out the intended outcome for a control that fails, times out or comes back inconclusive, or the decision is left to technical defaults.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Sequential validation checks
→ Parallel screening checks
→ Outcome for a failed, timed out or inconclusive control

The real requirement is not "Which controls do we run?"

It is "What evidence proves each control runs in the order the business chose?"

Have you seen an SLA missed because controls ran in sequence that could have run in parallel?
takeaway: Control order is a business decision, not a technical default. Sequential for validation, parallel for screening.

title: Treasury needed one answer before cut-off, and camt.053 could not give it
explain:
Treasury waits on a EUR 30 million Nostro credit before releasing an outgoing payment.

The cut-off is an hour away.

The team reads camt.053. It answers tomorrow, not today.

Here is how it happens:

→ Treasury waits for a Nostro credit
→ Outgoing payment is held until the credit arrives
→ camt.053 shows movements and balance at close of business
→ The decision must be made during the day
→ camt.052 intraday report or camt.054 notification can answer it

The assumption was:
"Read the statement."

Why?

The camt.053 statement holds the account movements and the balance at close of business, so it cannot answer a question that must be decided during the day.

Choose the message by the decision it must support, not by its definition alone.

BA Takeaway

Start from the business decision, then pick the message that can answer it in time.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Decision that must be made
→ Timing the decision needs
→ Message that can answer in time

The real requirement is not "Which report do we use?"

It is "What evidence proves the credit arrived before the cut-off?"

Have you picked a message by its definition, and found it answered the wrong question?
takeaway: Choose the message by the decision it must support, not by its definition alone.

title: A flawless pain.001, a USD 200,000 payment in the wrong engine
explain:
A customer sends a flawless pain.001 for USD 200,000.

It lands in an instant payment engine that handles EUR only.

The payment is held, delayed and then rejected, and the instruction was perfect.

Here is how it happens:

→ Valid pain.001 arrives
→ Routing rules are set by the payment business and applied by the acquisition layer
→ pain.001 provides the clues: instrument, currency and amount
→ The rules are incomplete, and the route is wrong
→ USD payment lands in a EUR-only instant engine
→ Payment is held, delayed or rejected

The assumption was:
"A valid message finds its own route."

Why?

The engine never invents or overrides the route. If the rules are incomplete or incorrectly applied, a valid payment can land in the wrong engine despite a correct customer instruction.

The message provides the clues, the rules decide the route.

BA Takeaway

Routing rules are a business responsibility. Test the rules against every instrument, currency and amount combination before they go live.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Message clues in pain.001
→ Routing rules
→ Engine assignment

The real requirement is not "Is the message valid?"

It is "What evidence proves the routing rules cover this payment?"

Have you seen a perfect instruction fail because the routing rules sent it to the wrong engine?
takeaway: The message provides the clues, and the business rules determine the route.

title: The API said 200 OK, and the EUR 80,000 payment was still rejected
explain:
An API call returns HTTP 200.

The EUR 80,000 payment is still rejected.

The call succeeded. The business decision failed.

Here is how it happens:

→ API call succeeds, HTTP 200
→ Account is open, so the first check passes
→ Account currency is EUR, and the product does not support FX
→ Fraud score comes back 95
→ Engine rejects the payment

The assumption was:
"HTTP 200 means the payment will succeed."

Why?

Technical success and business outcome are different things. Checking whether an account is open or closed is not enough if the engine also needs the account currency. A fraud score works the same way: the fraud system controls its scoring model, while the engine must convert the score into an action, above 90 reject, 50 to 90 process with a customer alert, and below 50 process normally.

API success is not a business decision.

BA Takeaway

Start with the business decision the process needs to make, not the API to build. Ask what information the engine needs to decide, then build the call around that.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Technical response
→ Business rules
→ Score to action mapping

The real requirement is not "Did the API succeed?"

It is "What evidence proves the engine has everything it needs to decide?"

Have you seen an API return success while the payment still failed?
takeaway: API success is not a business decision. Start with the decision the process needs to make.

title: USD 10,000 to India: one message, or two?
explain:
A US bank sends USD 10,000 to HDFC Bank in India, for an INR account.

One pacs.008 with settlement will not work. There is no direct relationship, and the settlement currency does not match.

The payment needs two legs, and the team sent one.

Here is how it happens:

→ USD 10,000 instructed from a US bank to India
→ No nostro account exists in the beneficiary bank country
→ Settlement currency differs from the payer account currency
→ pacs.008 goes without settlement
→ A separate pacs.009 cover must move the funds through an intermediary

The assumption was:
"Send one pacs.008 with settlement."

Why?

Serial and cover are infrastructure choices, not customer choices. Serial suits cases where correspondent or nostro accounts exist and the settlement currency matches the payer account currency. Cover suits cases with no direct relationship or a different settlement currency.

Serial or cover is a settlement decision, not a wording choice.

BA Takeaway

Decide by checking whether nostro accounts exist in the beneficiary bank country and which settlement systems the currency needs, such as Fedwire, TARGET2 or CHAPS.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Nostro accounts in the beneficiary country
→ Settlement currency against payer currency
→ Settlement system the currency needs

The real requirement is not "Serial or cover?"

It is "What evidence proves the settlement path fits the accounts and the currency?"

Have you seen a payment sent serial when the accounts and currency demanded cover?
takeaway: Serial or cover is a settlement decision, not a wording choice. Decide by accounts and currency.

title: The optional address field that cost EUR 12,000 in deductions
explain:
A pain.001 is sent without the sending business agent address and postcode.

The field is optional, so nobody captures it.

The beneficiary bank falls back to default values, and the EUR 120,000 payment arrives EUR 12,000 short after deductions and a compliance flag.

Here is how it happens:

→ pain.001 sent without the agent address
→ Field is marked optional in the message
→ Beneficiary or intermediary bank falls back to default values
→ Compliance issues, errors or deductions follow
→ Payment goes through, but short

The assumption was:
"Optional means not needed."

Why?

A field M, O or C status describes the message, while whether the information must be captured is decided by the business rules of the process. If the field is left out, the receiving bank may fall back to defaults.

A field status describes the message, not the process.

BA Takeaway

Always ask whether the field is needed for the process, rather than trusting the message status alone.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Message field status
→ Business capture rule
→ Default value handling

The real requirement is not "Is the field mandatory?"

It is "What evidence proves the field is captured when the process needs it?"

Have you seen an optional field left out, and the payment arrive short because of it?
takeaway: A field status describes the message, not the process. Ask whether the field is needed for the process.

title: The EUR 90,000 payment that waited for a check it did not need
explain:
A EUR 90,000 payment enters the engine.

Validation checks run one after another, as they should.

Then sanction screening, fraud screening, limit checks and risk checks also run one after another, for no reason at all. The payment is late.

Here is how it happens:

→ Payment enters the engine
→ Validation checks run in sequence and stop on first failure
→ Screening checks also run in sequence
→ Each screening check waits for the previous one
→ The payment is delayed, and the SLA is at risk

The assumption was:
"Run all controls in order."

Why?

Control ordering follows dependency. Validation checks such as account number and currency, name matching, account status and closure depend on each other, so they run one after another. Sanction screening, fraud screening, limit checks, risk assessment and regulatory checks have no dependency, so they can run at the same time.

Sequential for validation, parallel for screening.

BA Takeaway

The design question is which controls depend on each other and which do not, because that decides both speed and the stopping point.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Dependent validation checks
→ Independent screening checks
→ Stopping point when a check fails

The real requirement is not "Which controls do we run?"

It is "What evidence proves which controls depend on each other?"

Have you seen a payment delayed because independent checks were forced to run in sequence?
takeaway: Sequential for validation, parallel for screening. Order follows dependency.

title: Balance was enough, and the Rs. 25,000 payment was still declined

A customer tries to pay Rs. 25,000 by card.

The balance is sufficient. The payment is declined.

→ Funds check passes

The assumption was:
"Sufficient funds means approval."

The issuer checks card status, available funds or credit, transaction limits and fraud rules together. A payment can be declined even when the balance is sufficient, if a fraud rule or a limit is breached.

Sufficient funds alone never guarantee approval.

Design the decline to say which check failed, so the customer and the support team are not left guessing.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Card status
→ Funds or credit
→ Limits and fraud rules

The real requirement is not "Does the customer have the money?"

It is "What evidence proves which check declined the payment?"

Have you seen a customer told their card was declined, with nobody able to say which check failed?

title: The EUR 100,000 transaction with no audit trail
explain:
A EUR 100,000 transaction is screened and cleared.

Months later, an auditor asks for the evidence.

There is none. The control ran, but nothing proves it ran.

Here is how it happens:

→ Customer risk controls run
→ Transaction risk controls run
→ A case is escalated
→ The audit trail is incomplete
→ The control is treated as if it did not happen

The assumption was:
"We ran the control."

Why?

Anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing controls cover both the customer and the transaction, and an analyst must understand them well enough to write requirements that keep the audit trail complete. A control that cannot be evidenced is treated as if it did not happen.

Evidence is the control.

BA Takeaway

Write requirements that keep the screening outcomes, the case escalation path and the audit trail complete from the start.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Customer risk controls
→ Transaction risk controls
→ Case escalation and audit trail

The real requirement is not "Did we run the control?"

It is "What evidence proves the control happened?"

Have you seen a control treated as absent because the audit trail was missing?
takeaway: Evidence is the control. A control that cannot be evidenced is treated as if it did not happen.

title: EUR 150,000 cover sent to the wrong bank
explain:
A EUR 150,000 cover payment was sent.
The MT202 COV went to a bank that held no settlement account for it.
The funds landed where no one expected them, and settlement stopped.

Here's how that happens:

→ MT202 COV addressed to the wrong bank
→ Funds land in an account that was not expecting them
→ Beneficiary bank waits for a cover that never comes
→ Settlement stops

The assumption was:
"The address on the cover is an administrative detail."
The address is part of the settlement design.

Why?

In a chain, the MT202 COV is addressed to the bank that holds the account from which the funds will settle, and each bank addresses its own cover leg to the next bank that will fund it. Addressing the cover to the wrong bank breaks settlement.

The address is part of the settlement design, not an administrative detail.

What proves this cover was addressed to the bank that will fund it?

BA Takeaway

Address each cover leg to the bank holding the settlement account. Check the address before sending, and treat a cover that lands in an unexpecting account as a settlement break, not a delay.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Cover address
→ Settlement account holder
→ Next bank in the chain

The real requirement isn't "Was the cover sent?"

It's "What evidence proves this cover was addressed to the bank that will fund it?"

Have you ever traced a cover that landed at the wrong bank?
takeaway: The address is part of the settlement design, not an administrative detail.

title: EUR 130,000 cover, screened on one leg and missed on the other
explain:
A EUR 130,000 cover payment was screened and cleared.
The MT103 was checked. The MT202 COV was not.
The funds leg carried a sanctioned party, and the payment went through anyway.

Here's how that happens:

→ MT103 screened before credit
→ MT202 COV never screened
→ Sanctioned party on the funds leg missed
→ Payment credited, gap found later

The assumption was:
"Screening the instruction screens the payment."
The information leg and the funds leg are screened separately.

Why?

An MT103 and its MT202 COV are both subject to sanction screening, and the screening must happen before the payment is credited to the beneficiary. A hit on either leg stops the payment. A bank that screens only the MT103 and not the cover, or the reverse, leaves a gap that a regulator will find.

Screening one leg only leaves a gap a regulator will find.

What proves both legs of this cover payment were screened?

BA Takeaway

Screen the MT103 and the MT202 COV separately, before crediting. Stop the payment on a hit on either leg, and record both screening results on the case.

Keep these controls separate:

→ MT103 screening
→ MT202 COV screening
→ Hit on either leg stops the payment
→ Both results recorded

The real requirement isn't "Was the payment screened?"

It's "What evidence proves both legs of this cover payment were screened?"

Have you ever found a payment where only one leg had been screened?
takeaway: Screening one leg only leaves a gap a regulator will find.

title: EUR 40,000 MT103 STP stopped because one field used the wrong option
explain:
An MT103 STP for EUR 40,000 was sent to straight-through processing.
It stopped for manual handling.
One field had used an option other than A, and the system could not identify the bank.

Here's how that happens:

→ MT103 STP sent for straight-through processing
→ Field 57 uses an option other than A
→ System cannot identify the bank without human help
→ Payment stops for manual handling

The assumption was:
"Any option that names the bank will do."
An MT103 STP only allows option A for fields such as 52, 54 and 57.

Why?

Option A carries the party identifier and the BIC, so the receiving system can identify the bank without human help. Any other option leaves the bank to work out who the party is by hand, which is why those options are not allowed in an STP message.

Any other option leaves the bank to work out who the party is by hand.

What proves every party field in this STP message uses option A?

BA Takeaway

Use option A, with the party identifier and the BIC, on every party field in an MT103 STP. Check fields 52, 54 and 57 before sending, and treat any other option as a manual-handling case.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Field 52 option A
→ Field 54 option A
→ Field 57 option A
→ Straight-through processing achieved

The real requirement isn't "Does the field name the bank?"

It's "What evidence proves every party field in this STP message uses option A?"

Have you ever seen an STP payment stop over one wrong option?
takeaway: Any other option leaves the bank to work out who the party is by hand.
